Almost nobody lives along most of Australia's west coast because deserts reach all the way to the Indian Ocean—leaving thousands of miles of coastline without major rivers, fertile soil, or steady rainfall—while extreme heat, cyclones, and vast distances from the eastern cities have concentrated roughly 80% of Western Australia's 3 million residents into a single corner around Perth.
Although Western Australia covers a third of the entire continent (an area larger than Western Europe), its population is smaller than that of many individual cities, leaving the vast coastline north and east of Perth almost entirely empty.
Here is a geographic breakdown explaining why Australia's west coast lacks major cities outside of Perth:
10:56
Why Almost NOBODY Lives On Australia's West Coast
13K views · 1 month ago
YouTube · The Hidden Outbacks

1. The Desert Meets the Ocean (No Mountains, No Rivers)

• Missing the Great Dividing Range: Australia's east coast is backed by the Great Dividing Range, which catches moist Pacific winds and feeds reliable rivers and fertile farmland. Western Australia has no major coastal mountain range to capture rain, allowing the Great Sandy, Gibson, and Great Victoria deserts to spill right up to the coast.
• Ancient, Nutrient-Poor Soil: Much of Western Australia sits on the Yilgarn Craton—some of the oldest exposed rock on Earth. Over two billion years of erosion have stripped the soil of nutrients, making large-scale European-style farming nearly impossible outside the southwestern tip.
• Unreliable Water: Without snowmelt-fed rivers like the American West, freshwater is scarce. Even Perth relies heavily on desalination plants and deep groundwater to sustain its population.

2. Extreme Heat, Cyclones, and Unforgiving Seas

• Brutal Temperatures: Users on Reddit agree that extreme heat is a major barrier to settlement, with northwestern coastal towns like Onslow reaching over 50°C (123°F) and inland areas routinely exceeding 40°C (104°F).
• Tropical Cyclones & Flash Floods: While the central coast is bone-dry, the far north (the Kimberley and Pilbara) is battered by violent summer cyclones that dump torrential rain in a few weeks, carving rugged gorges and wiping out infrastructure.
• The Leeuwin Current: Unlike most continental west coasts where cold, nutrient-rich currents support massive fishing industries, Western Australia is washed by the warm, nutrient-poor Leeuwin Current, limiting coastal fisheries.

3. History, Isolation, and "Fly-In, Fly-Out" Mining

• A 40-Year Head Start in the East: Commenters on Quora agree that early Dutch explorers dismissed the arid west coast as barren, leading British colonization, ports, and capital to concentrate in Sydney and Melbourne starting in 1788.
• Extreme Geographic Isolation: Cut off from eastern Australia by the treeless Nullarbor Plain, Perth sits over 2,100 km (1,300 miles) from the nearest major city (Adelaide), making it one of the most isolated major cities on Earth.
• Mining Without Cities: As highlighted in GeoGlobe's overview of Western Australia and Superprof's population breakdown, the northern Pilbara region is a global mining powerhouse for iron ore, gold, and lithium. However, instead of building permanent cities, companies rely on automated ports and "fly-in, fly-out" (FIFO) workers who commute by plane from Perth's comfortable Mediterranean climate—a dynamic where opinions on r/geography are split on whether large-scale water infrastructure could ever justify expanding urban centers up the coast.
